title: Tea in the Dooars: gardens, workers and a long story
meta_description: How the Dooars became tea country after 1865: the first garden at Gazaldoba in 1874, Adivasi and Nepali workers, CTC tea, the railway and visiting a garden today.
summary: Tea arrived in the Dooars within ten years of the 1865 Treaty of Sinchula: the first garden opened at Gazaldoba in 1874, and by 1881 there were 55. Workers came from Chota Nagpur and Nepal, a railway followed, and today the Dooars grows mostly CTC tea, the strong granular kind in most Indian cups.

sections.heading: From Bhutanese plains to tea country
paras: Drive from Siliguri to Hasimara and you pass almost nothing but tea for long stretches: low, flat-topped bushes in neat rows, with tall shade trees spaced across them. It looks permanent, but it is recent. Until 1865 these plains were the Bengal Duars, held by Bhutan. After the Duar War and the Treaty of Sinchula in November 1865, they passed to British India and were organised as the Western Duars, joined to the new Jalpaiguri district in 1869.

The British saw land that was flat, well watered and lightly settled, close to Darjeeling, where tea had been planted since the 1850s. Within a decade the first Dooars garden was opened at Gazaldoba on the Teesta, in 1874, close to where the Gajoldoba barrage stands today. Others followed quickly. By 1881 there were 55 gardens, and the forests were being cleared and surveyed for more.

sections.heading: The people who built the gardens
paras: Tea needs many hands, all year. The Rajbanshi, Mech and other communities already living in the Dooars mostly kept to their own farms, so planters brought workers from far away. The largest numbers came from the Chota Nagpur plateau, in what is now Jharkhand and parts of Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Bengal: Oraon, Munda, Santhal, Kharia and other Adivasi peoples. Recruiters, called sardars, brought whole families, who settled in labour lines on the estates. Nepali workers came down from the hills to the northern gardens.

These families made the Dooars what it is. Sadri, a language of Chota Nagpur, became the common tongue of the tea gardens and is still spoken in the lines today. Adivasi festivals such as Karam, when a branch of the Karam tree is planted in the village dance ground and the community sings and dances through the night, are as much a part of the Dooars as the forests. Churches, Kali temples and sarna sacred groves stand within a few kilometres of each other in many gardens.

sections.heading: A railway, a club and a trade
paras: Tea needed a way out. Chests went by river at first, then by rail. The Bengal Dooars Railway, a private company, built lines across the plains from the 1890s, linking the gardens with the main railway and the port of Calcutta. Parts of today's line from New Mal to Alipurduar follow that early network.

Planters, many of them Scots, built bungalows on stilts and clubs in the larger estates. Calcutta agency houses managed many gardens and sold their tea at the city's auctions, which began in 1861. After 1947 most British companies sold out to Indian owners over the following decades, and many gardens are now held by Indian companies, while a growing share of leaf comes from small growers who sell green leaf to bought-leaf factories.

sections.heading: CTC, not Darjeeling
paras: The Dooars grows a different tea from the hills. Darjeeling's gardens, at 600–2,000 m, mostly make orthodox leaf tea, sold under a protected geographical indication. Dooars gardens, on the plains at 60–300 m, mostly make CTC tea: the leaf is crushed, torn and curled by machines into small granules that brew fast, dark and strong. It is the tea of the roadside stall and most Indian kitchens, made with milk and sugar.

Dooars bushes grow quickly in the heat and rain and are plucked from about March to November, with a pause in the dry, cool winter when the bushes are pruned. In March and April you see pluckers in the rows with baskets on their backs, and from the road the gardens turn bright green with new growth after the first rains.

sections.heading: Hard years in the gardens
paras: The story is not all tidy rows. Tea garden wages have long been low, and the Plantation Labour Act of 1951 put duties on owners to provide housing, water, medical care and schooling in addition to wages. When prices fell and some owners walked away in the early 2000s, a number of Dooars gardens closed or were abandoned, and reports of hunger and deaths in closed gardens made national news. Some have reopened under new owners; others remain troubled.

Wage rates, land rights for families who have lived in the lines for generations, and the future of small growers are still argued over in Jalpaiguri and Alipurduar. A visitor sees beautiful gardens; it is fair to know what life inside them can be like.

sections.heading: Visiting a tea garden
paras: Unlike Darjeeling, the Dooars has few gardens set up for tourists, and factories are working premises, not attractions. Most visitors see the gardens from the road between Malbazar, Chalsa and Binnaguri, or walk the estate roads around Samsing, Chalsa and Lataguri with a local guide. A few resorts are set inside tea estates and arrange garden walks. Ask before photographing workers, and never walk into the rows at dusk, when elephants and leopards use the gardens as corridors.
list: Best months to see plucking: March to May and again in autumn, from late September to November.
Good roads for garden views: Odlabari to Malbazar, Chalsa to Nagrakata, Binnaguri to Birpara.
Buy loose CTC from a local shop in Malbazar or Birpara rather than from gift tins.
Respect garden boundaries; estate roads are private, so ask the guard or your host first.

faqs.q: When was the first tea garden in the Dooars opened
faqs.a: The first Dooars tea garden was opened at Gazaldoba, on the Teesta near today's Gajoldoba barrage, in 1874. That was less than ten years after the Treaty of Sinchula in 1865 moved the Bengal Duars from Bhutan to British India. By 1881 there were 55 gardens in the Dooars.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Dooars and Darjeeling tea
faqs.a: Darjeeling tea grows in the hills at 600–2,000 m and is mostly orthodox leaf tea, with a protected geographical indication. Dooars tea grows on the plains at 60–300 m and is mostly CTC, crushed into small granules that brew strong and dark. CTC is the everyday tea of most Indian homes.

faqs.q: Who works in the Dooars tea gardens
faqs.a: Most workers are descendants of Adivasi families brought from the Chota Nagpur plateau from the 1870s onward, including Oraon, Munda, Santhal and Kharia people, along with Nepali families in the northern gardens. Sadri is the common language of the gardens. Many families have lived on the same estates for five generations or more.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit tea factories in the Dooars
faqs.a: Rarely. Dooars factories are working premises and few are open to the public. Some resorts set inside tea estates arrange garden walks and occasional factory visits for guests. Most visitors enjoy the gardens from the road or on walks with a local guide. Check current status before you travel.

CTC stands for crush, tear, curl, the machine process that turns tea leaves into small, hard granules. It brews quickly into a strong, dark cup that holds up to milk and sugar. Most of India's everyday tea, including most Dooars tea, is CTC. Orthodox tea, by contrast, keeps the leaf more whole.

faqs.q: What is Karam Puja in the tea gardens
faqs.a: Karam Puja is a harvest and nature festival of the Adivasi communities of the tea gardens, held in August or September. A branch of the Karam tree is planted in the village dance ground and worshipped, the Karam story is told, and people sing and dance to the mandar drum through the night. The next day the branch is lowered into a river or pond.

faqs.q: Why did some Dooars tea gardens close
faqs.a: Falling prices, debts and poor management led some owners to close or abandon gardens, especially in the early 2000s. Workers lost wages, rations and medical care, and reports of hunger and deaths in closed gardens drew national attention. Some gardens later reopened under new owners, while others still struggle.

faqs.q: When is the tea plucking season in the Dooars
faqs.a: Plucking runs from about March to November, with the busiest flush after the first rains in spring and steady growth through the monsoon. In the dry, cool winter, bushes are pruned and plucking slows or stops. March to May is the best time to see pluckers at work from the road.

faqs.q: Where can I see tea gardens on a Dooars trip
faqs.a: The road from Siliguri to Lataguri passes gardens at Odlabari and Malbazar, and the stretch from Chalsa to Nagrakata and Binnaguri is tea almost all the way. Samsing has gardens on hill slopes with views. Walk only on estate roads with permission, and keep out of the rows at dusk.
